questions.prompt: Which sentence puts enough in the right place?

options.text: The water is enough warm to swim in this morning.
The water is warm enough to swim in.
The water is enough warm for swimming in it.
The water is warm to enough swim in.

questions.explanation: enough follows the adjective, which gives warm enough — and that is what makes it the odd one out among the adverbs of degree, since quite, very and too all come before. Placing it in front of the adjective copies the position of very and too, which is the commonest mistake of the lesson and appears twice among these options. Putting it between to and the verb breaks the structure in a third way, since enough to must stay together. And repeating the object after the verb is unnecessary in any case: to swim in is complete as it stands.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 27, one of the six definitions is left over because it defines a different science. Which term does it really define: "the scientific study of animals and their behaviour"?

options.text: Ecology
Wildlife
The environment
Zoology

questions.explanation: The study of animals and their behaviour is zoology, and the definition sits in the exercise as the extra item because it looks very like the one for ecology. Ecology is the study of the relation of plants and living creatures to each other and to their environment — it studies relations, where zoology studies the animals themselves. Wildlife is not a science at all but the animals and birds, which is what the exercise defines in three words. And the environment names the natural conditions of land, air and water, not any study of them.

questions.prompt: Combine these two sentences: "The parcel is very heavy. We can't send it by post."

options.text: The parcel is heavy enough to send by post.
The parcel is too heavy to send it by post.
The parcel is not heavy enough to send by post.
The parcel is too heavy to send by post.

questions.explanation: The action does not happen and the reason is an excess of weight, which is exactly what too plus adjective plus to expresses. enough to would say the opposite, that the weight is sufficient for the parcel to be sent. not heavy enough gets the failure right but blames the wrong quality, since nothing here is missing. And repeating it after the verb doubles the object, because the parcel is already the subject of the whole sentence — that repetition is the single most frequent slip in this transformation.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using not only … but also: "Both his father and his mother are dead."

options.text: Not only his father but also his mother is dead.
Not only his father but also his mother are dead.
Not only his father and his mother are dead.
His father is not only dead but also his mother.

questions.explanation: When the structure joins two subjects, English makes the verb agree with the one nearest to it, and that is the subject after but also — his mother, singular, so the verb is is. Keeping are copies the agreement of the original sentence, where both made the subject plural, and it is the trap the book sets twice without ever explaining it. Replacing but also by and leaves not only without its partner and the sentence unfinished. And the last version joins dead to his mother, which are not the same kind of element at all.

questions.prompt: "The wind whispered through the trees at night." Which figure of speech is this?

options.text: A simile
A comparison of equality
A personification
A metaphor

questions.explanation: Whispering is something people do, and here it is given to the wind, which is exactly what a personification is. A simile would need like or as somewhere in the sentence, and neither appears — that one-second check is what settles most questions of this kind. A metaphor would say that one thing is another, as in the wind was a voice, and this sentence makes no such identification. And a comparison of equality is a grammatical structure, as … as, rather than a figure of speech at all.
